📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that closing statements in Rockstar and IWGB's employment tribunal case - revolving around the GTA 6 developer's alleged 'union busting' and the firing of 34 employees - have now been read, bringing the hearing to an end. There's at the moment no timeline for a verdict, however, with one commentator suggesting a judgement could take weeks or months to arrive.

The case, which began in September and has included evidence from 23 claimants in the months since, must now be considered by the judge, who will determine if Rockstar unfairly dismissed employees in breach of their employment rights. Rockstar has been accused of unlawfully firing workers for being part of a union, but the GTA developer insists employees were dismissed for breaching confidentiality agreements.

Recent findings suggest that people Makes Games' Chris Bratt has been following the case closely and reporting on proceedings as they've unfolded. With closing statements now complete, Bratt quoted Judge Lucy Wiseman as saying, "I cannot give a time frame for producing the judgement in this case. What I will say is that I will use my best endeavors to get that judgement out as quickly as I possibly can.".

However, Bratt suggests it could be ""anywhere from a few weeks up to a few months before we actually hear the judgement", noting "The firings themselves, let's not forget, happened over a year ago now. This has been a slog.".

According to recent reports, one fired Rockstar worker involved in the case spoke with Bratt after the closing statements to share their thoughts. "Honestly it's just sort of blended together," they noted. "It’s been so long, that after the first six months or so it became the latest depressing reality. I'm hoping the judgement will release us from it.".

Last month, the conclusion of the tribunal hearing was delayed after cross examination of witnesses ran long.

Yesterday's closing statements come at a time when all eyes are on GTA 6 as it finally releases this week, concluding years of development for both current and former employees. Many of those workers involved in the case urged players to support the game despite the legal dispute.

In a recent development, additionally, Rockstar employees are currently voting on whether they want recognised union representation at the studio. If the vote passes, it would be the largest recognised union across the entirety of the UK video game industry. The deadline for union votes is 26th November.

The Most Loved and Hated JRPGs by Fans

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1637 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dualshockers

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that JRPGs have long since become a distinct phenomenon as a specific subgenre of RPGs, even when they are not produced in Japan.
  • However, while there is a slightly more civilized consensus around what makes the best fighting game or racing game, the JRPGs fanbase always seems deeply divided.
  • I will alternate between hated and loved entries and avoid repeating franchises to keep the list dynamic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that JRPGs have long since become a distinct phenomenon as a specific subgenre of RPGs, even when they are not produced in Japan. Fixed characters, linear narratives, creative progression, and an atduesthetic usually inspired by anime are what tell us at a glance what makes a JRPG stand apart from any other subgenre under the role-playing umbrella. And to be honest, those exact elements are what draw me to the genre, sometimes removing one or adding another.

However, while there is a slightly more civilized consensus around what makes the best fighting game or racing game, the JRPGs fanbase always seems deeply divided. Some titles seem to sit at the same level of love and hate for fans, no matter which side you're on. That is why I decided to talk today about the most loved and most hated JRPGs by the public. This isn't a consensus or an objective truth, but a fun look at what I have observed after years on forums, debating with fellow JRPG lovers, and tracking the fanbase's overall perception.

I will alternate between hated and loved entries and avoid repeating franchises to keep the list dynamic.

Sources indicate that while I couldn't find a direct primary source confirming this claim, outlets like Kotaku and RPGFan say the same thing: due to Xenosaga Episode II flopping so hard, the series was cut from its intended six episodes to just three. For fans hoping to see Tetsuya Takahashi's vision fully realized, that was a massive blow and certainly left a mark of hatred on the second Xenosaga.

While Xenosaga Episode I: Der Wille zur Macht went over budget and featured far more cinematics than the average JRPG player was accustomed to (yeap), it was still a satisfactory experience. The second one? Not so much. The shift in art direction and the battle system genuinely pushed players away and, allegedly, led Bandai Namco to safeguard its investment by wrapping up the entire story as a trilogy. Much like Xenogears, Xenosaga became a beautiful what-could-have-been scenario, though luckily we eventually got to see Takahashi's ambitions realized with Xenoblade, which is still going strong.

In a recent development, to be completely honest, I am not that big of a fan of EarthBound. I played EarthBound Beginnings, also known as Mother, and found it impressive for an NES JRPG. Shortly after, I moved on to EarthBound, which I had played a long time ago and didn't remember much, and I walked away unimpressed. Maybe the American parody didn't resonate with me (I am not American), or maybe I played it too late, and the cultural zeitgeist didn't hit me the same way.

Industry observers note that even so, I fully recognize how much people who enjoy this JRPG truly adore it. They spare no praise, speak fondly of the experience, and admire not only the game itself, but also its creator, Shigesato Itoi. Many of those fans claim Mother 3, a title that never officially left Japan, is even better, but since I didn't vibe with the second entry, I have little interest in trying it.

Industry observers note that sometimes a game is hated for its themes, other times for an overly boring battle system, or perhaps because of an obnoxious character we cannot stand looking at. Occasionally, however, games draw hatred simply for feeling apathetic, failing to spark any real emotion in the player, and offering nothing particularly remarkable. That's exactly the case with Tales of Zestiria for many Tales fans.

Industry observers note that mind you, I actually enjoy the game, and it was the very first Tales of title where I earned the platinum trophy. I was never overly critical of Sorey's journey, the complex equipment fusion system, or even the misleading marketing around Alisha's protagonism. I mean, okay, fair enough, those all sound like completely valid points of criticism, yet I still had a good time. Not everyone can say the same, and whenever you look at a Tales of tier list, Zestiria almost always sits right at the bottom.

According to recent reports, apparently, there are two types of fans in the JRPG world: those who love Suikoden II and those who haven't played it yet. I am not kidding here. I considered adding Xenogears to this spot because I know it has a very vocal fanbase, quite scary to be honest, borderline toxic. But Suikoden? That feels like a genuine relationship, a true love situation. Every time you meet someone who notes Suikoden II is their favorite game, you can practically see their eyes light up.

It has been revealed that to a large extent, I get it! Suikoden II is awesome. The grounded political plot stood out at a time when countless games were mostly about slaying God in a high fantasy setting. The 108 recruitable characters, each carrying their own motivation and reason for joining the resistance. The six-party-member battles with combo skills, and so on. Okay, you might need to use a walkthrough to recruit everyone and unlock the true ending, but the journey itself is already wonderful, and Luca Blight is a terrific villain. What is there not to love, right? Glory to Suikoden.

Sources indicate that there is nothing more miserable than watching a series you love, follow closely, and appreciate in every detail slowly fall from grace. For me, that didn't happen with Star Ocean, because I genuinely love Star Ocean: The Divine Force, though that is precisely how many felt after Star Ocean: Till the End of Time, the third entry. Plenty of fans didn't care for Star Ocean: The Last Hope yet could still stomach it, but Star Ocean: Integrity and Faithlessness? Just mentioning the name makes me feel your glare.

The fifth Star Ocean suffered from an affliction that hit many JRPG franchises during that era: constricting budgets. I know that doesn't excuse its final quality, but it is the reality. The game severely lacked traditional cutscenes, playing out almost entirely through real-time in-engine camera angles, not out of artistic charm, but due to a lack of investment. I still like the game for two reasons: Item Creation remains incredible, and as someone who loves constantly swapping between party members, being able to deploy everyone into battle at once was a blast, even if having seven party members acting simultaneously got confusing and felt like a bit too much. It had a chaotic family reunion vibe, you know.

In a recent development, out of all the JRPG fans I know, well over half say they discovered or fell in love with the genre after playing Final Fantasy VII. That fact alone could summarize this entire entry, because you either know someone just like that or you are that person yourself. I am a bit older, so I played other JRPGs before FFVII, though my cousin fits that exact mold, since he still uses an email address with the game's acronym in his handle to this day.

It is completely understandable, mind you. Final Fantasy VII was a global phenomenon that paved the way for JRPGs to gain worldwide recognition. That is why if you watch footage from the E3 showcase where the remake was unveiled, you will see countless explosive reactions. I know many newcomers to the genre or franchise don't understand why Square Enix split the remake into three parts, calling the company mercenary (fitting for the game's plot, to be honest). Yet, I believe Square did it to honor the franchise's legacy, deliver something fresh for longtime fans, and naturally attract a new audience who can experience that same magic veterans felt when they first played and fell in love with it.

In a recent development, whereas with most entries I listed as most hated (not hated by me, remember!) I tried to soften the blow and use euphemisms to avoid insulting people who enjoy those games or the developers behind them. For Lunar: Dragon Song, though, the gloves are completely off. I had only heard rumors about it, about how this mechanic was terrible and that feature was lousy, until one day I decided to test it for myself.

Good lord, it is awful. So many baffling design decisions make me genuinely wonder how anyone let them pass. First, and most obviously, simply running in the game drains your HP. I mean, what? Then there are two separate reward modes per battle, one granting only experience points and another granting only loot. I didn't understand that system at first and left loot mode active, feeling bizarrely weak despite fighting endless battles. On top of that, combat has mandatory auto-targeting, plus a bland story, forgettable characters, and other uninspiring features. Lunar: Dragon Song is universally hated, and it deserves every bit of it.

Industry observers note that whenever someone asks me which JRPG I would recommend to a complete newcomer to the genre, the answer nine times out of ten is Chrono Trigger. Pointing to a 1995 release even today speaks volumes about the work's enduring relevance and timelessness. And I will go a step further: that recommendation doesn't rely on cheap nostalgia alone, because Chrono Trigger truly is a spectacle, with pacing, gameplay, and design that can captivate even the most stubborn skeptics who resist JRPGs.

It has been revealed that and of course, among JRPG enthusiasts, it is tough to find anyone who doesn't genuinely love Chrono Trigger. You might have critiques about it (I certainly do), or complain about one small detail or another. Still, it's nearly impossible to deny that it is a masterpiece and a majestic blueprint for building a JRPG. It stands undeniably as the most beloved JRPG of all time, even if you don't happen to be one of the people who love it.

#143670. Latest Update: I Hate Video Game Romance – Here's Why Grand Theft Auto VI Is The Exception

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (890 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gameinformer ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: I Hate Video Game Romance – Here's Why Grand Theft Auto VI Is The Exception

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (890 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gameinformer

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, generally speaking, I do not like romance mechanics in video games.
  • If you've played Baldur's Gate 3, Stardew Valley, Date Everything, or practically any other game with romance options, you're familiar with the gameplay loop.
  • In a recent development, many games structured like the ones above are written as well as they can be.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, generally speaking, I do not like romance mechanics in video games. I never find them convincing. Relationships build way too quickly, and usually all it takes to win someone over in an RPG or farming sim is a couple of conversations and a few gifts. In Grand Theft Auto VI, however, I'm extremely invested in the romance between Jason and Lucia, and it comes down to the game's quieter moments and slice-of-life mechanics.

If you've played Baldur's Gate 3, Stardew Valley, Date Everything, or practically any other game with romance options, you're familiar with the gameplay loop. I ask an NPC about her hometown, sympathize with her tragic backstory, promise to be there for her, and then give her the book, cake, or mining resource she likes. Do it enough, and one day she'll approach me with the uncharacteristically heartfelt confession that she can't stop thinking about me. The process is too transparently mechanical: I can scan the dialogue options and instantly know which of the three sentences will boost my affinity rating the most. It feels less like an actual relationship and more like a long-term scheme to program someone into dating.

In a recent development, many games structured like the ones above are written as well as they can be. The issue is scope and structure. Romantic relationships are nuanced and unique, but there often aren't enough resources during a game's development to represent more than the basic building blocks. Players are meant to suspend disbelief and fill in the gaps – even though you technically only spoke to that villager a few dozen times, you're married with a child, so you imagine it's actually been years.

Of course, this scope is the difference between Grand Theft Auto VI and these other games – Rockstar made time and space for everything in this world, and romance is no exception.

Since they're dating when the game begins, Jason and Lucia admittedly skip the courtship phase that many games focus on, but their relationship is still conditional and malleable – if you want them to like each other, you should be acting in their best interests. And while the mechanical aspect of their romance is still plenty visible, the actions to increase that meter are vastly expanded. There has been a lot of discussion about the early game, when you can prep for Lucia's release from prison by buying flowers or groceries, and while I like those gestures, they're not what sold me on the relationship. Say what you will about modern dating standards, but flowers and food are too easy – too obvious for me to feel connected to and invested in a couple.

When I played this section, I felt like Jason's hair looked a little unkempt, so I got a shave and a haircut. And, to my surprise, this improved his relationship with Lucia. She wasn't around and wouldn't see the results until later, but it still scored me partner points, as did repairing the roof, painting the bedroom walls, and even giving Jason's car a newly introduced paint job. These unexpected, specific tasks don't just fill up the relationship gauge – they communicate information about both characters. Lucia is really looking forward to getting out of prison, and having a finished house and a clean, put-together partner sets her in a better mood. Meanwhile, my actions establish that my version of Jason knows she likes these things and would do them without even asking.

It has been revealed that minor, specific tasks like these are romantic because they imply a degree of thoughtfulness that sidesteps the grand gestures expected of a long-awaited reunion. Yes, there should be apples in the fridge, but that's a basic need; knowing the exact conditions Lucia wants the house to be in makes me believe Jason actually knows her. It becomes even more effective – both in real relationships and in the credibility of the in-game partnership – when thoughtfulness is demonstrated on a day-to-day basis, in the quiet moments.

Grand Theft Auto VI is a long game with a slow, steady pace, leaving room for the intimate interactions other games wouldn't have time for. If you come home at the end of the day and see your partner watching TV, you can sit next to them and get a bonus. When they go to sleep, they'll call out to you and ask you to lie in bed and scroll on your phone with them. You can hold hands in public, buy each other clothes, and remember to text back promptly. There are large, dramatic moments and professions of love, yes, but players are likely to experience vastly more of these minor interactions than those scripted cutscenes.

In a recent development, romance can be flashy, but it has to be more than that. It's nice to see the starring duo dance, drive, and shoot at foes during cutscenes. But it's the long car rides when Lucia reassures Jason that her mom likes him, or the evening on the couch when Jason talks about how he likes the way Lucia laughs, that make this relationship work narratively.

What are your favorite video game romances? Let us know in the comments!

In a recent development, while a portion of Deadlock's player base is busy getting ready to celebrate the holiday, Valve has released another massive patch with a unique Thanksgiving-themed twist. Acting as a follow-up to Deadlock's limited Halloween event, the newest update detailed on Deadlock's Steam Page brings countless balance changes, quality-of-life improvements, features, and some themed mechanics to get players into the holiday spirit.

One of the most notable features of the limited-time event is a series of massive parade floats right outside the window, leading all the way down Blue Lane and visible right after loading into Deadlock's lobby. Aside from being simple decorations, these balloons also introduce a upcoming mechanic by dropping Turkey dinners that can be collected for a new buff.

While the parade doesn't do much to start, after three minutes, refreshing crates will spawn hanging beneath them that drop the Turkeys when destroyed, alongside the chance of dropping additional goodies like buff items or Souls.

After eating a Turkey, you'll immediately gain two stamina and the 30-second Stuffed buff, granting you 5 percent Bullet Resist, 5 percent Spirit Resist, and progressively healing you for a total of 90 health. 20 minutes into a match, the health increase jumps to 90 instantly, and 170 over the 30 seconds.

You don't just want to go around eating every Turkey you can, however, as eating another while you have the Overstuffed buff will disable sprinting and give you 60 percent stronger gravity.

While the limited-time event is certainly a fun change, especially considering its real-life counterpart of the Macy's parade got delayed, the real meat (pun intended) of the update comes from the patch notes that have now gone into effect, with a few of the following changes being some of the big highlights of the update:.

While these are only a small percentage of the changes introduced in the fresh update, you can find all of the new adjustments on Steam's official Deadlock patch notes page, which also includes 166 individual nerfs, tweaks, and buffs, most of which affect the following heroes:.

While there are too many Deadlock changes to list them all here, I would definitely recommend checking out the patch notes if you play any of these characters or have had trouble facing them in the past.

Industry News: Stalker 2’s first expansion officially revealed, and it's taking us to the power plant where it all began

📅 26 Mar 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (309 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Vg247

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, one of the biggest reveals out of today’s Xbox Partner Preview showcase has been the upcoming Stalker 2 expansion.
  • Cost of Hope is the major news; a new add-on that the developer has wisely decided to reveal fairly close to release.
  • First off, Cost of Hope is set for release this summer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, one of the biggest reveals out of today’s Xbox Partner Preview showcase has been the upcoming Stalker 2 expansion. The developer did tease some sort of announcement ahead of the event, but I don’t think an expansion was on many of our bingo cards.

Cost of Hope is the major news; a new add-on that the developer has wisely decided to reveal fairly close to release. Or, at least, the planned release target.

First off, Cost of Hope is set for release this summer. It’ll arrive on all current platforms simultaneously, meaning PC, Xbox, and PlayStation. The expansion is described as “non-linear”, and it takes place in the heartlands, deeper into the Zone.

The story revolves around a conflict between Duty, and Freedom, two factions whose idea of the what the Zone is and their understanding of its possibilities differ widely. You’ll be playing as protagonist Skif once again, and the expansion’s events will run parallel to the main game.

In a recent development, GSC Game World says Cost of Hope will introduce two upcoming regions, offering dozens of hours of gameplay. We’ll get to actually explore the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant as part of the expansion, alongside the Iron Forest.

Each of the two latest regions will have its own hub area, NPCs, quests, activities and stories. Of course, it wouldn’t be a Stalker expansion without some new weapons, and Cost of Hope promises a few - some can even be seen in the trailer.

It has been revealed that the developer also confirmed that there’s one other story DLC in the works. Together with Heart of Chornobyl, and Cost of Hope all three will form a trilogy of interconnected stories. More details on Cost of Hope - including a release date - will be revealed sometime in the summer.

Pocket monsters, just not those ones.

Sources indicate that pre-registration only opened at the end of October, so Bandai hasn't kept anyone waiting long. Digimon Alysion is out now on iOS and Android, finally putting the Digimon Card Game on your phone.

Recent findings suggest that expect an original story with a brand latest cast of characters, plus a few Digimon you won't have come across before. It's built to teach you the rules as you play through it. The tutorial covers how cards are laid out and used, along with the basics of a battle.

Recent findings suggest that your collection mixes cards from the physical Digimon Card Game with fresh ones made for Alysion. On top of that, you’ve got Shiny Cards, Alt-Art Cards and Premium Alt-Art Cards (the animated ones), and you'll get one free pack a day to build your decks from.

According to recent reports, once you’ve fleshed out your kit, you can take it into ranked against people from around the world, or keep things relaxed and spar against friends and characters from the story instead. Breeding is back as well, for that matter. You can raise Digimon and Digivolve them all the way up to Mega, and there's a Digidex of more than 100 entries to fill in.

Industry observers note that pokémon TCG Pocket is the obvious comparison, and probably the reason Digimon Alysion is arriving now at all. The difference is that Bandai isn't starting from scratch, and if you've been playing the physical version, you'll recognise a fair bit of what’s part of your packs.

Bandai has already done something similar with Dragon Ball's Fusion World, which you can play digitally and on paper, so it's a fairly safe bet the game is meant to send some people towards the physical cards too.

Digimon Alysion is free-to-play with in-app purchases on the App Store and Google Play, and a launch event, Battle Carnival Dukemon Ver., is running now.

SteamDB will add "affiliate links to authorised game retailers" and a newly introduced tab dedicated to mods, first revision since Nexus Mods takeover confirms

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in a first substantial update since acquiring SteamDB from its founders back in September, the owners of Nexus Mods have outlined some latest additions coming to , the two sides in the deal have announced some additions coming to the community-run backend database.
  • "We're now a couple of months in since [the takeover] announcement, so I thought it was about time we shared a quick revision on what we've been working on behind the scenes, along with a few changes you'll start to see rolling out over the coming weeks," Victor Folmann, CEO of Nexus Mods owners Chosen wrote in a blog post on SteamDB.
  • It has been revealed that there are two main new features he pointed to that you'll notice popping up on SteamDB soon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in a first substantial update since acquiring SteamDB from its founders back in September, the owners of Nexus Mods have outlined some latest additions coming to , the two sides in the deal have announced some additions coming to the community-run backend database. Affiliate links aimed at providing options to help folks find the cheapest price for a game and a new tab dedicated to the mods Nexus host for a game are incoming, as work on behind-the-scenes improvements continues.

"We're now a couple of months in since [the takeover] announcement, so I thought it was about time we shared a quick revision on what we've been working on behind the scenes, along with a few changes you'll start to see rolling out over the coming weeks," Victor Folmann, CEO of Nexus Mods owners Chosen wrote in a blog post on SteamDB.

It has been revealed that there are two main new features he pointed to that you'll notice popping up on SteamDB soon. The first is one that anyone could have seen coming, a new tab on each moddable game's page that shows off some mods hosted for it on Nexus Mods and a host of modding-related data. "The new tab will help you discover mods for games you're browsing on SteamDB, making it easier to see whether a game has an active modding community and explore what it has to offer," Fomann wrote. "For now, we'll only be showing mods from Nexus Mods, as we already have access to that wealth of modding data, making it a straightforward starting point for this new feature.

In a recent development, "We appreciate that some of you might be wondering why we're not including Steam Workshop, too. It's certainly something we'd be open to exploring as we develop the feature further, along with other modding sources. With that in mind, if you run a modding website and would be interested in having your community's mods included, we'd love to hear from you.".

Recent findings suggest that that seems perfectly fine, but the other incoming feature's a bit more controversial given SteamDB's historically not been all about the money. "One thing we've seen people ask for is an easier way to find the cheapest place to buy a game, and we're now working on making that possible," Folmann wrote. "We'll be introducing affiliate links to authorised game retailers, giving you more options when looking for the best available price on a game.

Sources indicate that "We recognise that introducing affiliate links may raise some concerns, so we want to be clear about how they'll work. First and foremost, as I mentioned, we'll only feature authorised retailers; we will not be including grey-market resellers. We've also made a deliberate decision about how prices are displayed: retailers will be ordered by the cheapest available price in your currency, not by whichever retailer offers us the highest affiliate commission. If a retailer doesn't offer pricing in your currency, we'll still show deals in other currencies provided they are available in your region.".

Industry observers note that folmann was clear in the initial announcement of the takeover that Nexus Mods' bosses would be actively looking into ways SteamDB could make more money to sustain itself, so the addition of these links isn't out of the blue either. Whether SteamDB regulars agree that they're a "lighter-touch" way of earning the site some cash without detracting from the traditional experience of using it is another matter. I'll need to see how I feel once I've actually navigated a few pages with the links in as part of looking up stuff about games, but my first instinct is that as long as the pages don't end up revolving around the links and it's still easy to get to the info you want without interacting with them, I probably won't be too put out.

Beyond those tweaks, Folmann mentioned "improvements to how updates are tested before they go live" and how swiftly the team can react to issues have been among the less obvious work going on behind the scenes. "We're still in the early stages of what we want to achieve, and there's plenty more work we need to do and would like to work on," he wrote in closing.

Folmann and co only took over Nexus Mods in June last year, making them still relatively upcoming custodians of both it and SteamDB.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As GTA 6 finally arrives, increasingly outspoken games industry legend Warren Spector - known for seminal immersive sims including Deus Ex - has offered both praise for the game's achievements and lambasted its "billion dollar" development model, writing, "I just hope GTA 6 is the last of its kind even if it’s the best we have to offer".

Sources indicate that spector revealed his retirement from games development in August following struggles at his OtherSide Entertainment studio, and has been vocal about the state of the games industry in the months since, notably saying anyone at EA responsible for the "travesty" of BioWare's closure should be "ashamed". And now Spector has taken on GTA 6.

"First, congratulations to everyone who worked on GTA 6. It looks like it will be a high point of sorts for our medium and our business," he wrote in a post on LinkedIn. "However… its billion dollar development cost and an undoubtedly crazy marketing budget don't represent a business model anyone else can or probably should emulate.

According to recent reports, "That's especially true," Spector continued, "when thousands of developers are out of work. A billion dollars pays for a lot of games and a lot of salaries. Personally I'd rather have hundreds of games and full employment than one game no matter how amazing it is.".

Industry observers note that the "sure success" of GTA 6 proves a point he's made "for years", he said: "That no game that matters ships on time and/or on budget". Highlighting GTA 6's year-long delay and reported billion dollar budget, Spector suggested, "Give a game the time and money to prove its potential (key word, potential) and you have a chance of making something great. Underfund a game or force it out the door before it's ready [is] guaranteed failure no matter how much potential it has.

"So, again, congratulations," Spector concluded. "Ambition and innovation are necessary for the medium to reach its potential. I just hope GTA 6 is the last of its kind even if it's the best we have to offer.".

Despite Spector's concerns, GTA 6's arrival is, as expected, already causing shockwaves across the industry. It has broken pre-order records for Xbox and PlayStation stores, smashed the all-time livestream viewer record, and apparently briefly broke Reddit too. And is its success deserved? Eurogamer's Chris Tapsell thinks so, saying it "pushes back the horizon of video games once again" in his five star GTA 6 review.

Industry observers note that today’s Genshin Impact Special Program has wrapped up, and it’s brought us some significant news about the next major update. Luna 6 is the next phase in the action RPG’s story, titled Song of the Welkin Moon: Rondo - Augured Homecoming.

It’s set to arrive on April 8, bringing with it a tonne of latest content, including a major expansion to the original region of Mondstadt.

As part of this upcoming update, Mondstadt’s northern parts expand with new areas. The new Dornman Port is one thing, but the most exciting is the Temple of Space. This floating structure is home to Asmoday fragments, and is made up of different realms inspired by Liyue, Sumeru, and various other civilizations from around Teyvat. Launching with the update is a new mechanic that lets you manipulate the space to reveal hidden paths containing secrets.

In a recent development, if you take the time to explore, you’ll find a lot to there to learn about Asmoday, Ruler of Space. There’s a latest boss to take on in the temple, too: Watcher: Fallen Vigil.

Sources indicate that the only new character in Luna 6 is Linnea, who continues the current trend within HoYoverse games of focussing heavily on cute pink-haired animal-themed girls. Linnea is a 5-Star Geo Bow user who can really work with parties made up of Lunar-Crystallize characters, with her substantial gimmick being the ability to turn Hydro-Crystallize reactions into Lunar-Crystallize reactions.

Linnea has a companion, Lumi, who allows her to increase the Lunar-Crystallize damage she deals, while also lowering her enemies’ Geo resistance. Linnea can also deliver either off-field Geo damage or a Lunar-Crystallize reaction hit with her Elemental Skill.

Recent findings suggest that beyond that, she can heal the party using her Elemental Burst. If you take Linnea with you as you explore, she can help you discover rare animals, thanks to her innate naturalist abilities.

This upgrade will also see Chasca get her first-ever rerun, and you’ll be able to roll for her in the first phase of Event Wishes. The second phase will feature no newly introduced characters and instead focus on Nefer and Lauma. There’s going to be another Chronicled Wish banner, this time specifically for Fontaine characters.

You can look forward to a few other fresh arrivals in Luna 6, including The Nod-Krai Trade Expo, some quality of life updates to Miliastra Wonderland to up the number of players in each lobby, not to mention various other UI changes.

Final Fantasy Resonance Devs Are Somehow Surprised That Fans Still Like Turn-Based Combat

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (360 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Nintendolife

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Final Fantasy Resonance was met with high praise when it launched on 22nd October 2026, earning a score of 8/10 from us and a critic average of 85 over on Metacritic.
  • Despite being an adaptation of a somewhat middling mobile title, Resonance's focus on turn-based combat mixed with the handsome HD-2D visuals made it an instant fan-favourite.
  • This comes via an interview at Game Spark with producer Keisuke Nakashima, co-producer Miki Kimura, and director Hiroto Furuya (thanks, Automaton), who all feel that Resonance's reception exceeded their expectations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Final Fantasy Resonance was met with high praise when it launched on 22nd October 2026, earning a score of 8/10 from us and a critic average of 85 over on Metacritic.

Despite being an adaptation of a somewhat middling mobile title, Resonance's focus on turn-based combat mixed with the handsome HD-2D visuals made it an instant fan-favourite. The developers, however, seem somehow surprised at the positive reception, believing that opinions would be a bit more divided.

This comes via an interview at Game Spark with producer Keisuke Nakashima, co-producer Miki Kimura, and director Hiroto Furuya (thanks, Automaton), who all feel that Resonance's reception exceeded their expectations.

Nakanishi-san said, “I think the action-oriented and 3D Final Fantasy games are wonderful too, but I was surprised to see just how many people, not only in Japan but overseas as well, are eager for the kind of FF they remember from back in the day, with classic turn-based battles and pixel art.”.

Development actually focused on appealing to more old-school fans of the series, with Nakanishi stating that the intended direction was for Resonance to feel almost like a follow-up to Final Fantasy 6. "We figured it was something we ourselves would enjoy, and that there would be players out there who’d feel the same way", he mentioned.

With the series being so heavily focused on 3D visuals and action-oriented gameplay in recent years, the team simply didn't expect Resonance to have such mainstream appeal.

"I thought this was a rather unconventional title, so I expected opinions on it might be divided", said Kimura-san. "I think the fact that a game with such an unusual background has been embraced by so many people is a positive for the industry as a whole, and I’m personally very happy to see it.”.

In a recent development, hopefully the positive reception will lead to more original games being made that focus on turn-based combat and 'retro' visuals. There's clearly a demand for it!

Did you pick up Final Fantasy Resonance on Switch or Switch 2? What do you make of it? Leave a comment and let us know.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As AI usage during game development and discussions surrounding it become more prominent, Ubisoft has been taking a firm stance on embracing it.
  • In a recent development, according to a report yesterday from Vertical Slice, the firm has been enforcing generative AI usage across its development teams in order to increase productivity and enhance the project in general.
  • However, Ubisoft has now responded to the original reporting, stating that while they do encourage AI usage across all production stages, it doesn’t mean that they require every single project to implement it, as they still need to be added only when it actually makes sense.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As AI usage during game development and discussions surrounding it become more prominent, Ubisoft has been taking a firm stance on embracing it. But according to the firm itself, the usage of such tools is more like a suggestion than a rule to be strictly followed.

In a recent development, according to a report yesterday from Vertical Slice, the firm has been enforcing generative AI usage across its development teams in order to increase productivity and enhance the project in general. And if you choose not to implement it, you would have to justify your choice.

However, Ubisoft has now responded to the original reporting, stating that while they do encourage AI usage across all production stages, it doesn’t mean that they require every single project to implement it, as they still need to be added only when it actually makes sense.

The original version of Vertical Slice’s report states that, after speaking with various employees (who chose to remain anonymous due to possible backlash), Ubisoft is looking forward to increasing its gen-AI usage across all titles. If they choose not to use it, they have to detail the reasons for their choice. Otherwise, their ideas wouldn’t be approved to be worked on.

Industry observers note that the report came out days after Ubisoft announced that their newest studio, Motherbrain, would be an AI-focused studio, being an key part of their “newly introduced operating model”. The announcement also came days after over 160 staff members were let go from their positions in Canada-based studios.

According to Ubisoft, they are simply encouraging their “teams to explore where AI can be useful and bring value to their work.”.

While it all seems daunting and terrifying, the studio decided to step up to clarify exactly what it all means. According to Ubisoft, they are simply encouraging their “teams to explore where AI can be useful and bring value to their work,” and ensuring that no employee is being silently forced to implement gen-AI in their work.This aligns with a claim from one of the employees Vertical Slice spoke with. According to them, while they aren’t outright mandated to use AI in their projects, the firm has fully decided to implement it whenever they have the chance.

According to recent reports, while "AI psychosis" has been a thing for a while, it’s undeniable that the existence of generative tools has greatly shifted the industry and its inner workings in just a couple of years. From waves of layoffs followed by AI-pilled initiatives and the implementation of disclaimers about its usage on official game store pages, it’s hard not to be alarmed by all of these signals.

Ubisoft has been a huge player in these changes. The fresh Motherbrain studio is a byproduct of Teammates, an AI experiment from last year. This AI-powered demo uses the tool to mold your experience according to your voice and actions, as NPCs will react to your commands and, as stated on their official site, “allow players to experience the story in their own way”.

Recent findings suggest that with all of these fresh advances in mind, it’s not unexpected to see such a posture from the company. However, it doesn’t mean they should be free of criticism when it's due. It’s hard not to associate all of the previously mentioned layoffs (which have been ever more common in the industry) with the increasing fear of being replaced by AI.

Another Ubisoft employee also mentioned feeling “cornered by generative AI all the time” since the recent attitude shift from the higher-ups, implying that some pressure over AI usage does exist inside the firm.

This doesn’t mean that Ubisoft’s own statement is incorrect. It could simply be a different way of perceiving attitudes and decisions taken by the firm. But with so many AI-related incidents across the industry, such as the recent wave of AI game copies, it’s hard not to be worried about the future of gaming.

Breaking: "It’s hard not to worry": Even as GTA 6 launches on console amid glowing reviews, Rockstar devs are already concerned about getting laid off

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (753 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It's widely expected to sell more copies than main character Lucia Caminos has skin pores, more copies than there are words even in Eurogamer's five-star review, which I believe Chris Tapsell has written specifically to exhaust and destroy such neurones as I have remaining.
  • In an article supporting this month's union vote at Rockstar North, one of the game's animation programmers argues that "workers across the sector are helpless to resist the waves of redundancies crashing around us, until we get organised.".
  • Recent findings suggest that the animation programmer in question is Nestor Uriarte, writing in The Guardian's Comment Is Free section.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GTA 6 launches on console today. It's widely expected to sell more copies than main character Lucia Caminos has skin pores, more copies than there are words even in Eurogamer's five-star review, which I believe Chris Tapsell has written specifically to exhaust and destroy such neurones as I have remaining. And yet, staff at Rockstar Games are apparently worrying about being laid off, as development winds down and investors start to bicker about Line Going Up Even More.

In an article supporting this month's union vote at Rockstar North, one of the game's animation programmers argues that "workers across the sector are helpless to resist the waves of redundancies crashing around us, until we get organised.".

Recent findings suggest that the animation programmer in question is Nestor Uriarte, writing in The Guardian's Comment Is Free section. Following some personal reflections on his time at the studio, he calls on other Rockstar devs to get behind the union, describing it as both "a huge step forward" for a manufacturer that has previously faced allegations of "crunch culture", and a win for UK game developers at large. "What happens here could open the door for other workers across the UK to imagine an alternative future for the industry – one in which workers’ voices are taken into account more," Uriarte writes.

Sources indicate that the vote at Rockstar North will run till 26th November, and could give rise to a union spanning over 1600 developers, according to umbrella organisation the Independent Workers of Great Britain. If that comes to pass, it would make the Rockstar union the largest recognised videogame developer union in the UK.

It has been revealed that it comes as the tech giant and a group of fired workers await the result of an employment tribunal battle over alleged "union-busting". Rockstar has accused the workers in question of "gross misconduct" and a breach of confidentiality by means of a union Discord server. Amongst other things, the legal brawl has revealed that Rockstar had a mole on that server for two and a half years, prior to the firings.

As for the prospect of further job losses, after GTA 6 goes on sale, Uriarte cites a wave of mass layoffs across the industry that has affected the creators of even commercially successful games like Battlefield 6 and Netflix's FIFA World Cup.

"After the significant day, we have had no indication that layoffs are coming, but it’s hard not to worry about what the future holds," he writes. "Studios across the industry have been slashing huge portions of their workforces, with an estimated 24,000 roles axed globally over the last two years. It claims a lot about the industry that even my colleagues and I, working on the biggest game of all time, are worried about getting laid off. But the truth is that workers across the sector are helpless to resist the waves of redundancies crashing around us, until we get organised.".

The obvious context here is that GTA 6 has been a massively expensive production, with a development team headcount in the thousands. While one could accuse Uriarte of fear-mongering, I do find it hard to believe that executives at parent company Take-Two aren't weighing up some timely "down-sizing" right now. In general, videogame companies have a long tradition of axing the books once a game has been shipped, despite arguments that keeping experienced teams intact often pays off. In Rockstar's case, however, it's also worth bearing in mind that the GTA 6 rolling out this week is only part of the package. There's also the hazy prospect of the next incarnation of GTA Online, which – going by GTA 5 sales – will be a money spinner for many years, and will require a sizeable staff to maintain. Oh, and of course there's the PC version.

Echoing many peers, Uriarte also argues in his piece that it's important to unionise now in order to negotiate proper protection against generative AI cost-cutting initiatives. "The rapid emergence of AI is transforming how studios work and raising fundamental questions about the future of our industry," he continues. "Across the sector, the skills that workers spend years developing risk being devalued as their creative work is replaced by AI.

"Rockstar has noted it is committed to preserving jobs and it has been clear that our games will continue to be made by people," Urirarte concedes. "But with recognition we’d have a seat at the table to manage this industry-wide transition together.".

Breaking: Does GTA 6 have an 'easy mode'? Not officially, but there are two very important settings you can change to make the game less difficult

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (568 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By now, you've probably heard that you cannot use cheats in GTA 6 until you complete the main story.
  • But, for anyone looking to have a slightly easier time with GTA 6 than the dev's intended experience, I come with good news: you can make the game a little bit easier by toggling two options in the game's Settings menu.
  • It has been revealed that 'Accessible Combat' decreases enemy health and makes them deal less damage to your character — the kind of rebalancing that you'd expect from a traditional difficulty slider.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By now, you've probably heard that you cannot use cheats in GTA 6 until you complete the main story. Not only that, but enabling cheat codes also locks story progression and deactivates the ability to save. Basically, you can use cheats to have a quick crime spree and blow off some steam, then it's back to normalcy. Understandably, some gamers are a little put out with this change.

But, for anyone looking to have a slightly easier time with GTA 6 than the dev's intended experience, I come with good news: you can make the game a little bit easier by toggling two options in the game's Settings menu. If you open Settings, and then navigate to Gameplay, you'll find 'Accessible Combat' and 'Reduced Vehicle Damage' toggles. You can activate both to make GTA 6's more difficult elements a little bit easier to work through.

It has been revealed that 'Accessible Combat' decreases enemy health and makes them deal less damage to your character — the kind of rebalancing that you'd expect from a traditional difficulty slider. 'Reduced Vehicle Damage', as you'd expect, lowers the damage taken by your vehicle and allows your ride to endure more punishment. This applies to gunfire, environmental threats, and impact damage.

Industry observers note that toggle these settings comes with a warning from Rockstar, though. A prompt notes that enabling these modifiers will "significantly change the balance and experience of the gameplay". I've been playing around with these settings and whilst they are not a foolproof 'God Mode' by any means, you can absolutely see a difference in the game when they're enabled: Jason and Lucia take a lot more punishment from melee damage and gunshots, and I had to really try to get Jason's old banged up pickup into even the 'slightly smoking' bracket of disrepair. Your mileage may vary, but these settings, from what I can tell so far, certainly do make the game easier.

According to recent reports, given that cheats disable trophies and progression, these settings might be something to keep in mind if you're trying to find a smoother path through the main story of GTA 6. It's a credit to Rockstar's accessibility teams that these have been included at all - alongside the 23 other gameplay accessibility options, the 12 display options, the 70 UI options, the 24 camera options, and the 14 audio options.

It has been revealed that "We create inclusive, intuitive, and immersive experiences for every player," noted Rockstar's associate UI director, Sam Grosset, in materials provided to Eurogamer ahead of the game's launch. "Accessibility is considered from the outset, and designing for diverse needs enables us to create better games for everyone. We wanted every player in GTA 6 to have options to play the game how they like. Whether it's selecting a larger font size, opting for a more minimal screen experience, or making a controls tweak to sprinting... the choices are open to all.".

We also learned yesterday that Rockstar has made GTA 6 missions "harder to fail" by making them more open-ended, and giving players more ways to figure out how to do things in their own way.

If you need a hand with any of the myriad things GTA 6 asks you to do, you can read Eurogamer's Grand Theft Auto 6 walkthrough as well as a breakdown of Grand Theft Auto 6 cheats.

In a recent development, but it is important to go in with the right expectations because, thanks to Sony, you lose a couple of things too, namely, waking the console and haptics of any kind. Yep, thanks to Sony's licensing rules, any third-party controller, no matter how official, will have no vibration at all, and won't be able to wake the console up. Personally, these things are important, but I think the trade-off for the extras you do get makes it worth it.

Rockstar’s Rob Nelson Explains Why You Can’t Wield GTA 6's Chainsaws

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (562 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thegamer

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • GTA 6 is being celebrated for more reasons every day, and rightfully so.
  • Sources indicate that rockstar producer Rob Nelson revealed the level of thinking that went into not only some of the endless things you can do in Leonida, but also some of the things you can’t in an interview with VGC.
  • “As far as the chainsaw – I think it would have been too much for this game at this resolution and these characters,” Nelson explains, adding, “It’s not a resource thing.” Other omissions, such as not being able to play games like darts or bowling, were confirmed to have been left on the cutting room floor because Rockstar simply didn’t think it was worth the time and effort when those resources could be put to better use elsewhere.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GTA 6 is being celebrated for more reasons every day, and rightfully so. However, the most striking thing about the game, since it’s the first thing you see and it’s hitting you over the head every second you’re looking at it, is how stunning it is. That realism is one of the reasons why the option to make Jason and Lucia hyper-violent is taken out of the player’s hands.

Sources indicate that rockstar producer Rob Nelson revealed the level of thinking that went into not only some of the endless things you can do in Leonida, but also some of the things you can’t in an interview with VGC. One of the things Nelson discussed was the decision to not include weapons that would allow for a heightened level of violence that have been present in previous GTA entries, like chainsaws and katanas.

“As far as the chainsaw – I think it would have been too much for this game at this resolution and these characters,” Nelson explains, adding, “It’s not a resource thing.” Other omissions, such as not being able to play games like darts or bowling, were confirmed to have been left on the cutting room floor because Rockstar simply didn’t think it was worth the time and effort when those resources could be put to better use elsewhere.

The realism that you get with GTA 6 means even standard stuff that has to be in the games, like shooting someone or hitting them with a blunt object, is far more visceral than it has ever been before. When coupled with how much more grounded GTA 6’s lead characters are, giving them the option to carve someone up with a chainsaw just doesn’t fit.

“Even at the most psycho, did Jason and Lucia really need that – what’s that going to look like?” Nelson continues, adding, “You’re always trying to find what is the right sort of line and the right balance, it really just depends, you want to feel like you can interact with as much of the world as possible,” when asked about chainsaws existing in Leonida, but Rockstar choosing not to let players interact with them at all.

It has been revealed that it’s a tricky line to walk. A huge part of GTA has always been about players doing whatever they like, and going “psycho,” as Nelson puts it. Once I was done with GTA San Andreas's story, I input cheats to give pedestrians weapons and then made them riot. The whole point of that game for me after that was for it to be as chaotic and unrealistic as possible.

Recent findings suggest that that was a long time ago. Sure, GTA has always been violent, but its violence has never been realised with the same realism as it is in GTA 6. Not just the way it looks, but the way you play and the repercussions that come along with everything you do. Jason and Lucia are the closest the series has ever seen to protagonists that act like real people. They’re not caricatures like the leads in previous GTA games. They might be criminals, but as Nelson indicates, they’re not psychos who are going to fight their way out of a situation with a chainsaw. It wouldn’t make sense for them, and it no longer makes sense for GTA.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When you’re making a major budget video game, it's likely different members of staff and development teams are going to clash. Be it creative differences, long-term team structure, or even post-project follow-through, no unit is a legion, and these split opinions can easily shape not only the title itself, but the future of everyone who worked on it.

Rockstar has faced public inquiries into the health of its developers over the monumental Grand Theft Auto 6, and union rumors have floated for weeks. With the vote finally coming through rejecting the recognition of remarked union, one staff member, named Thomas March, came out to explain why he thinks the team is better off without it, at least for now.

In a recent development, discussion of the union representing Rockstar staff has been a rumor mill for weeks, with no clear answer about what's happening behind the scenes. Following an internal vote handled by a third party, Rockstar staff voted not to establish the IWGB as their union of choice, while maintaining the option to establish a union of their own at a later date.

In a post clarifying exactly what went down behind the scenes, Thomas March, an associate principal developer at Rockstar, described the IWGB’s position on Rockstar staff’s treatment as “endlessly frustrating…”. To March, the Independent Workers’ Union of Great Britain represented a bottleneck in staff voices, stopping individuals from arguing for their own benefits individually.

According to March, Rockstar’s worker treatment is nothing short of industry-leading. “Nowhere else have I been listened to so closely, treated with such respect, even while working with veterans and experts bar none.” Thomas claims that Rockstar’s treatment of each individual staff member means that formal recognition of a union isn’t really necessary.

When you’re making a major budget video game, it's likely different members of staff and development teams are going to clash.

Between flexible hours, employee benefits, and a truly caring workplace, March paints Rockstar as the fledgling developer’s dream, all the while decrying other staff members who raised complaints over crunch and questionable conditions of their own.

Industry observers note that rockstar staff does have its own internal union, dubbed the RSGWU, but the IWGB would have granted the staff unprecedented protections and argumentative power. While March cited the independence as a major boon, unions only get results when a staff force is unified. For now, they’ll have to make do with the RSGWU, a decent union that seems to have granted the team their own voice amongst investors.

The general response to March’s defense of the vote has been less than glowing, with dozens of fellow devs and union members decrying the result as short-sighted and selfish. Amidst the clapbacks and dismissals are former coworkers and industry peers lamenting a squandered chance, describing their own negative experiences with Rockstar’s internal face.

In a recent development, at the end of the day, each and every person can only share their individual experiences, each of which will paint their biases in a major deciding vote like Rockstar’s. The nature of the vote means that, should conditions fail to improve for everyone, members of Rockstar staff can try to recognize another union, or empower their current union to fight for their rights more actively.

Whether you believe Rockstar is a bastion of developer health or a corporate machine aiming for quality over all else, at current each individual member of Rockstar staff will need to choose.

Independent negotiations or small-scale union building is all they have at present, and while the recognition of the IWGB in such a prestigious studio could have made major waves, every individual is sure to vote for their own future.

#143645. Tech Report: I have double-checked and yes, original 'GTA killer' Driv3r really was that rubbish

Tech Report: I have double-checked and yes, original 'GTA killer' Driv3r really was that rubbish

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1218 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • At this point the tragedy of Driv3r, or Driver 3, or my personal favourite Drive-thrur, is well thumbed.
  • According to recent reports, A more widely forgotten detail is that, for a while, there was a non-zero chance - a belief, even - that Drive Three Er was going to be the opposite.
  • Sources indicate that you likely know the rest, though one of the dangers of familiarity is the subsequent breeding of complacency, which in this case can manifest as a thawing acceptance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At this point the tragedy of Driv3r, or Driver 3, or my personal favourite Drive-thrur, is well thumbed. A familiar litany of unrealised ambition, heinous bugs, dull open-world design, and an expensive yet audibly bored voice cast, the accidental comedic highlight of which is Michelle Rodriguez flatly reeling off car theft orders from what sounds like the inside of a Michelle Rodriguez-sized tupperware container.

According to recent reports, A more widely forgotten detail is that, for a while, there was a non-zero chance - a belief, even - that Drive Three Er was going to be the opposite. The 2003-2004 hype cycle had sowed the notion that this would in fact be the open-world crime thriller to knock Grand Theft Auto off its perch, and even 22 years before GTA 6's idolising reviews, that was no small promise; Rockstar were still enjoying the balmy success of Vice City, and we could see San Andreas cresting the hill on a stolen, shining BMX. "Ah, but did they have Michael Madsen doing doughnuts in car parks?," publishers Atari asked the world, either unaware or in denial of the spluttering, clapped-out rattletrap they were about to wheel into the showroom.

Sources indicate that you likely know the rest, though one of the dangers of familiarity is the subsequent breeding of complacency, which in this case can manifest as a thawing acceptance. I succumbed to this myself, having recently installed a legally unlinkable copy of Drivethreeuh, mind opened to the possibility that maybe it wasn't that bad. Six hours later, I am here to tell you: it was.

Almost nothing here works, figuratively and literally. Within three minutes of the opening mission, before Madsen's undercover cop Tanner goes undercover, you're ordered to join some marked police cars to head for a bust – but because the rozzers' primary function is to give chase to you, later on, driving too close crosses their wires, provoking them into blue-on-blue ramming maneuvres. Later, in a motorbike sprint down an inexplicably exploding beach, cartel goons are positioned across the sand, presumably to take drama-enhancing pot shots. They're so slow, however, both to notice your presence and to physically raise their guns, that they're barely out of their idle animations by the time you whizz past. And your own guy isn't much better: an assassination mission, which ends with your target cornered from an elevated position, requires that you take a few steps backwards first, as Tanner can't drop his shootin' arms low enough to land a hit from the balcony he's on.

Industry observers note that unlike Vice City's Tommy Vercetti, he can at least swim, which by 2004 standards gives the seaside Miami and Nice maps a fair verisimilitude, particularly when a shot-up boat engine forces the abandoning of ship. No amount of product-of-its-time concessions, though, can account for how woodenly unpalatable the on-foot action is. Controls are stiff and shooting feels meaningless, with zero tangible sense of bullets being sent nor received; killing a man carries all the weight of just shouting at him to lie down, and if it weren't for sound effects and the dwindling health bar, I could park Tanner in front of a firing squad of identically-modelled thugs with almost zero impression that his lungs were filling with Uzi rounds.

It has been revealed that driver, of course, began as a pure wheelman sim, later installments only letting you hoof it after someone at developers Reflections began smelling that Rockstar money. It was therefore always unlikely, even for the purported GTA killer, that this would achieve action-adventure sophistication in its bipedal bits. Even so, god, it's woeful. Stingy checkpointing also means that failure is often punished by having to replay those tedious, flavourless shootouts in full.

The driving is better, which is a bit like saying there's decent cheese in this cheese and smallpox toastie. It's reasonably slidey, when throwing the back end through a curving French alleyway, and in contrast to the gunplay, there is a somewhat realised tactility to ploughing around in two tonnes of rolling metal. It has problems of its own, mind. Cars feel okay when they're moving, but contact and crashes are leaden, sluggish, visually underwhelming occasions that I would call non-events, were they not so slow to recover from that a single nasty impact can scupper a timed mission. Granted, I quickly re-learned how vital it is to keep both eyes on the road, as other vehicles, pedestrians, lamposts, and other detritus tend to pop into existence some mere fifty feet in front of my speeding bumper.

The result, of both this graphical shortcoming and the overly punishing crashes, is a getaway car sim that too often encourages you to drive like cataract-ridden grandparent. Worse, whoever put Letty Ortiz in a lunchbox must have also been in charge of the engine noises, producing an array of miserable high-rev dins – especially for the motorbikes, which screech like amateurishly autotuned vacuum cleaners. There are also shades of that deranged cop AI in ordinary commuters, who I've repeatedly seen swerving and slaloming around empty lanes, seemingly for no reason beyond violent confusion.

Strangely enough, my 2026 return has largely dodged the game's infamous glitchiness, the worst instance of physics defiance being a garage door that appeared to lift Tanner into the air before propelling him, incorporeally, through the car shed's roof. I recall much worse, from the days when I'd have my dad rent it for me from Blockbuster. Mission-critical NPCs getting stuck on walls; flipped pursuit cars spinning endlessly; getting flung into space when walking on an overturned vehicle (a common occurrence, given the actual 'crawling out' animation sometimes failed to play, the game instead teleporting you onto the spring-loaded underside instead).

Recent findings suggest that I've thus far escaped these, but as far as I know, they're still lurking dormant, and none of what I've witnessed with adult eyes has been funny or stupid enough to imbue Driv3r 3 The Third with a Wiseauean so-bad-it's-good quality. It's just bad. It was always bad. Why did I even entertain the possibility that it wasn't bad?

In a recent development, reflections, to their credit, accepted their folly. Narratively unrelated sequel Driver: Parallel Lines tucked away a bin full of discarded copies, at least until Ubisoft bought up the series and patched it out, and for all the fantastical coma silliness of direct followup Driver: San Francisco, that was sensible enough to keep Tanner where he best belongs: hands on the wheel, foot on the gas, gun holstered. And was a far, far better game for it, too.

As 2011's San Francisco launch also remains the most recent Driver release, I regretfully can't end with the assurance that DrIIIver's legacy is a mere blip on a redeemed franchise. That stain stank, and did for ages, very possibly to the extent that GTA's one-time biggest rival never recovered.

Still, even if Reflections couldn't fully turn around their fortunes, the consistent improvement from this to Parallel Lines to San Francisco showed that they did learn something. Maybe so too did anyone else who went on to make an open-world action game. Which wouldn't be the worst outcome; after all, those who do not learn from gnarled, stinking wrecks like this are doomed to repeat them.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

HoYoverse just wrapped up a stacked Honkai: Star Rail Special Program, delivering the one-two punch of revealing the game’s next major update, and detailing what you can expect from its third anniversary celebrations.

According to recent reports, first off, Version 4.2, dubbed So Laughed the Masses, arrives April 22, making two characters playable, and bringing back a host of beloved characters for re-runs. The newly introduced enhancement continues the Phantasmoon Games arc, as the story takes an especially suspect new development.

It has been revealed that the substantial inciting incident of this new chapter is the reveal that whoever wins the Phantasmoon Games will also become the permanent Aeon of Elation. Meanwhile, Fulwish has invited all Supplicants to the Fulwish TV HQ to announce their intention to host a TV debate about the ultimate goal of the Phantasmoon Games.

Naturally, you’re invited, and you’ll have to overcome the challenges that await to gather more Wishpower.

In a recent development, our first new arrival is Silver Wolf LV.999, with whom you should already be familiar from her Version 1 form. The difference now, of course, is that she’s getting a brand-new alternate kit, since — true to her new name — she's evolved into a Godmode Player upon reaching Level 999. Silver Wolf LV.999 is a 5-Star Imaginary character on the Path of Elation.

Recent findings suggest that her main combat trick is the ability to rack up Hidden MMR, which is what allows her to eventually activate her Cartridge and settle into the aforementioned Godmode state. While in that form, she shifts the entire battle into the virtual world, pulling in both teams into her gaming domain.

In a recent development, this is essentially a world under her control, which is why she can unlock a Reward Stage at the start of her turn, which lets her spawn in-game items. When picked up, these items can turn the tide of battle.

Keeping up with the ultra-gamer persona, Silver Wolf's Aha Instant strike blasts all enemies with a laser cannon, dealing massive damage. Perhaps her most interesting ability is being able to hack into the battlefield when she’s not actively on the team, something she can do when a teammate falls under enemy control.

Evanescia is the other newly-playable character, who has thus far only been an observer of the Phantasmoon Games, as well as one of the most prominent upcoming characters we've met so far on Planarcadia. V4.2 sees the girl join the roster as a 5-Star Physical character who’s likewise on the Path of Elation. As she fights, she always accumulates Certified Banger, when she earns the title she’s able to simultaneously regenerate Energy and maintain her damage.

Evanescia’s damage continues to increase the more Certified Banger she accumulates, triggering an attack from Master Fox upon reaching a certain threshold, which deals damage to all enemies and regenerates Energy for herself. Her Elation Skill adds a bit of a performance to her kit, and is capable of hitting all enemies.

Recent findings suggest that you may have noticed the Path of Elation theme in this one, so you won’t be surprised to learn that the Elation Trailblazer variant on the main playable character is also joining the team in 4.2. There’s a new weapon that starts off as a glow stick but can transform into a lightblade as you deal damage, and, yes, gain Certified Banger.

It can also turn into nunchucks, which delivers a unique flurry of attacks on all enemies surrounding the character, dealing multiple instances of damage. You can also use it to cheer for a teammate, hyping them up.

Recent findings suggest that version 4.2 Warp Events will bring back six characters. The first half will see reruns of The Dahlia, Castorice, and Firefly. The second half will give you another shot at unlocking Tribbie, Sunday, and Feixiao. What’s more, four of the game’s characters will be buffed in this patch, so you may want to reconsider putting them them back on your team. They are Firefly, Huohuo, Seele, and Welt.

It has been revealed that as part of the same revision, you can expect the debut of the Cosmic Data Roaming event, which goes live alongside the anniversary celebrations. The event lets you live the life of a streamer.

Currency Wars is getting a massive expansion, too. Likewise, the Cosmicon Collective is getting its version 2.0 update, adding new decks, dice as well as a new team challenge game mode.

Sources indicate that elsewhere, you’ll find fresh items in the Gift of Stardust Store, including a new outfit for Castorice. Between the time 4.2 debuts and when the celebrations begin, you’ll be able to try your luck in Aha's Chosen: Spreading Elation Everywhere, an online event where you can leave a message for a chance to win various prizes.

Exoprimal, Capcom's Dinosaur Hero Shooter, Will Go Offline And Become Unplayable Next Year

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (358 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Gameinformer

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Capcom has been on a truly generational run in recent years, but even their legendary lineup of games was bound to have a few stumbling points.
  • It has been revealed that "Thank you so much for your continued use of Exoprimal," an announcement on the Exoprimal site reads.
  • Sources indicate that between now and September 29, Capcom will bring Exoprimal down in stages.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Capcom has been on a truly generational run in recent years, but even their legendary lineup of games was bound to have a few stumbling points. Exoprimal is a prime example – the dinosaur-themed hero shooter was not a terrible game by any means, but it requires online play and hasn't managed to maintain much of a player base. Today, Capcom announced plans to sunset the game, rendering it unplayable by September of next year.

It has been revealed that "Thank you so much for your continued use of Exoprimal," an announcement on the Exoprimal site reads. "We regret to announce that service for Exoprimal will be discontinued as of 8:00 PM (PDT) on Wednesday, September 29, 2027." The announcement goes on to specify that the game will "no longer be playable" after that date – Exoprimal is an online-only game which requires an internet connection, so once the servers are offline, that's it.

Sources indicate that between now and September 29, Capcom will bring Exoprimal down in stages. As of yesterday, players can no longer purchase a Survival Pass Premium Tier for seasons 1-4. On March 30, Exoprimal and all its DLC will be de-listed from stores, but software owners can still play it and/or re-download it. Finally, the game will fully shut down by September 29.

Any online-only game has a finite lifespan, but it's still sad to see them go. Many gamers are frustrated in recent years because it feels like they don't really own anything, whether it's a subscription-based product or a digital download that can be discontinued at a moment's notice. It's the primary cause of outrage behind PlayStation's decision to stop producing physical discs in 2028.

As for Exoprimal, our reviewer Marcus Stewart largely enjoyed his time with it, writing, "Exoprimal’s creative subversion of expectations impressed me in more ways than one, and its approach to telling a robust narrative within a multiplayer framework is an example I hope other titles study. I just hope it’s enough to keep the game from going extinct.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We already knew there'd be a frantic clamour for GTA 6 this week, and we also knew plenty of players would be eyeing up Xbox's 'New Zealand trick' to get in on the action early. But it's now being reported that a whopping 2m UK and US players took advantage of the trick - which, for context, equals more than a third of New Zealand's actual population.

Here's a quick bit of background: Rockstar's regional release schedule meant GTA 6 launched at midnight on 19th November everywhere, local time. As such, New Zealand was the first country in the world to see the hugely anticipated game go live, thanks to timezones. And because Xbox players can make purchases on any regional store easily, simply by changing their console's country, understandably impatient sorts opted to become temporary virtual New Zealand residents in their droves (on PlayStation, the process requires a regional account and payment in local currency so is more finicky).

According to recent reports, in fact, according to data analytics firm Ampere Analysis, the early demand was such that 1.5m Xbox owners in the US and 600,000 UK Xbox players briefly went Kiwi for the occasion of GTA 6's launch. Other countries highlighted by Ampere include Canada, where 200,000 Xbox players took the New Zealand plunge, Brazil (200,000 players), and Mexico (100,000 players).

By contrast, just 100,000 PlayStation players in the US opted to dive in early, reflecting, as Ampere notes, "the ease of being able to switch country in the account settings on Xbox consoles." And here's all that info in graph form:.

Recent findings suggest that amusingly, Upcoming Zealand's tourist board tipped a wink to the sudden influx of virtual 'visitors', telling them "We'd love to have you". It also cheekily offered a video of cheerful tourists admiring the country's resplendent natural beauty "Life," read the accompanying caption, "because we're getting GTA 6 first.".

In a recent development, some hours later and the rest of the world can now finally, officially join in the GTA 6 fun, and it's a game worth playing. Eurogamer's Chris Tapsell called it an open world of "awe, minute detail and impossible scale" in his five star GTA 6 review. And if you need some help getting through the game now it's here, you can check out Eurogamer's Grand Theft Auto 6 walkthrough as well as a breakdown of our Grand Theft Auto 6 cheats.
